name: Djaru
catalog_citation: Tsunoda, Tasaku. 1981. The Djaru Language of Kimberley, Western Australia. Pacific Linguistics B-78. Canberra: Australian National University.
catalog_locator: section 2.7 'Stress and Pitch', pp.47-48 (PDF pp.69-70 of the sealang PL-B78 scan)
catalog_quote: Phonetically, both stress and pitch occur but they are 'phonologically irrelevant or nondistinctive' (Trubetzkoy 1969:31) in Djaru; they do not differentiate meanings of words (as the English stress or Japanese pitch). A few of their phonetic features may be mentioned. STRESS generally falls on the first syllable of a word: ḍáḍi 'kangaroo' (W), máŋari 'vegetable food'. The same applies to bimorphemic or longer words, i.e. compound or reduplicated words, or words with derivational suffix(es) (see Chapter 6): búja-jaṇi ... máŋa-maŋa ... ŋába-jaṛu 'water-HAVING'. However, the (first syllable of the) second morpheme (as well as the first morpheme) can receive a stress if: (a) it is trisyllabic or longer; or, (b) (in the case of a disyllabic morpheme) it contains a CVC syllable. In fact, in such a case the second morpheme receives a prominent stress more frequently than the first morpheme. S…

(2) The classification rests on the standard reference grammar of Djaru (PL B-78, 1981, 290 pp), first-hand fieldwork; (3) fetched sources Senge 2015 (Wanyjirra, ANU PhD, open): it agrees on initial primary stress, non-contrastiveness, and morpheme-initial stress in compounds/reduplications/long suffixes, but treats the non-initial long /aː/ as attracting SECONDARY stress (ˈbaˌlaarn) in §2.7 while §2.2 says /aː/ 'receives a stress wherever it occurs'

sources.citation: Senge, Chikako. 2015. A Grammar of Wanyjirra, a language of Northern Australia. PhD thesis, Australian National University. xxv+732 pp. hdl:1885/109341
sources.quote: p.101: 'Stress in Wanyjirra is characterised as increased loudness, and sometimes, length although it is not phonologically contrastive. Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the phonological word. If the word contains more than three syllables, secondary stress generally occurs on the penultimate syllable.' sources.note: Only modern full grammar in the Glottolog list for jaru1254 (sister variety Wanyjirra); its stress section gives the same lexeme balaarn 'turtle' with PRIMARY initial and SECONDARY on the long vowel (ˈbaˌlaarn), where Tsunoda transcribes Djaru [baláːɳ] (rarely [bálaːɳ]) — directly relevant to how firmly the CVV-attracts-stress clause should be coded; also adds a penult secondary-stress statement absent from Tsunoda.
